goals: Use an RBF kernel and tune gamma and C
why: Kernels let a linear method draw curved boundaries without explicitly creating thousands of features. The same idea appears in Gaussian processes and kernel PCA.
explain: Some data cannot be separated by a straight line, such as one class in a ring around another. Map the points into a **higher dimension** (add z = x² + y²) and a flat plane separates them.
The **kernel trick** computes similarities as if the data were in that higher space, **without ever building it**. That is cheap even for infinite-dimensional mappings.

The **RBF (Gaussian) kernel** is the default. Its **gamma** sets how far each point's influence reaches: large gamma gives very local, wiggly boundaries (overfitting); small gamma gives smooth boundaries.
Tune **C and gamma together** with a grid search on a log scale (0.001, 0.01, 0.1 …).

formula.plain: RBF similarity: 1 for identical points, falling towards 0 with distance; gamma (γ) controls how fast it falls.

example.title: Lifting one-dimensional data
steps: Seven parts, deviation from target size (mm): −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3. Parts within ±1 mm pass; the rest fail
Failures sit on both sides of the passes, so no single threshold on x works
Add the feature x²: 9, 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, 9. Passes have 0 or 1; failures 4 or 9
One flat cut at x² = 2.5 separates them; back in mm that is −1.58 < x < 1.58, a two-sided rule
example.result: One curved feature turned an impossible straight-line problem into an easy one. Kernels do this lift implicitly, for many features at once (the same idea as z = x² + y² for a ring).

mistakes: Large gamma + large C → memorising the data.
Using kernel SVMs on very large data (quadratic memory).
takeaways: RBF is the default; tune C and gamma together
Powerful on small to medium non-linear problems
use: Non-linear boundaries on small to medium datasets

practice.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_circles
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
X, y = make_circles(400, noise=0.1, factor=0.4, random_state=0)
print(SVC(kernel="linear").fit(X, y).score(X, y))
g = GridSearchCV(SVC(kernel="rbf"), {"C": [0.1, 1, 10], "gamma": [0.1, 1, 10]}, cv=5).fit(X, y)
print(g.best_params_, round(g.best_score_, 3))
